studies.title: Sparks Struck At Dawn
studies.meaning: Five lines of pure motion, and not one of them names a rider. Each closes on a verbal noun of manner, so the Arabic gives the action and then the way it is done: running, and the sound of breath; striking, and the spark; arriving, and the hour of it. Commentators differ over what is being sworn by. Most read war horses at a dawn raid, and a well-known early reading takes them as the mounts of pilgrims moving at speed. The two readings disagree about the animals and agree about the pace.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan by the majority of the classical sources. Horses were expensive and comparatively uncommon in Mecca, kept for raiding rather than for work, and the dawn attack was the standard form: ride through the night, strike as the light comes up, be gone before any defence can be organised. The sources record no occasion for the surah and spend their discussion on what the oaths refer to.

keyTerms.note: A word for the sound a horse makes breathing hard at speed, and it occurs only here in the Quran. It is a noise rather than a movement, so the oath opens with something heard before anything is seen.
The verbal noun for striking a flint to draw fire. Applied to hooves on stone it supplies the only thing visible in the dark, which is why the daylight in the next line lands as a change of scene.
From a root of something raised and left hanging in the air. It occurs only here, and it marks the moment the raid becomes visible at a distance to the people who are about to be hit.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A raid was an economic instrument rather than a battle. Riders covered ground at night, struck a camp at first light while the herds were still gathered and people were asleep, drove the animals off and left. Hearing hooves before dawn meant a family's entire wealth was walking away from them. Nobody in the audience needed the scene explained, and many had stood on one side of it or the other.
studies.didYouKnow: The first five lines each end in a verbal noun in the same grammatical case, and three of those five words occur nowhere else in the Quran. That is an unusually dense run of rare vocabulary for so short a passage, which is one reason the classical lexicographers discuss this opening at such length before any commentary on its meaning begins.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The oath is sworn on the audience's own image of excellence. Speed, nerve, coordinated force and animals bred for exactly this were what that society admired most and organised itself around, and the passage takes all of it as a witness before turning the argument against the people who prized it. The effort that gets the sympathy in these five lines belongs to the animals, and the riders are not described at all.

crossReferences.why: Names horses among what was made for people to ride and as an adornment, from the same created order.
Opens another surah with a series of oaths on pure motion whose referent the commentators also dispute.
Shows Solomon with horses at evening, another passage where the animals and their speed carry the scene.

studies.applyIt: Tomorrow morning, before you look at anything, listen for one minute and count what you can identify by sound alone. Traffic, a bird, a door, someone else's routine. The surah begins with a noise in the dark and only reaches daylight three lines later, which is roughly the order in which a day actually arrives.

studies.title: The Ledger Of Losses
studies.meaning: The charge is stated and then, unusually, the accused is called as the witness against himself. Scholars differ over that line, some reading God as the witness and some the human being, and the sources record both. A third statement follows about the intensity of love for wealth. Then two verbs of the last day, and the pairing is exact: what is in the graves is scattered out, and what is in the chests is gathered in.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a short surah that opens with five lines of galloping horses raiding at dawn, striking sparks and raising dust. The turn from that scene to a statement about human ingratitude is abrupt and unexplained, and the classical commentators connect the horses to a raiding party without agreeing which. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: A rare word occurring only here. Classical readers gloss it as one who counts misfortunes and forgets favours, and it is also used of ground that grows nothing, so the image is barren rather than hostile.
A verb for turning something over and emptying it, used of a container upended. Applied to graves it makes the earth give up its contents rather than the dead climbing out.
A verb for separating a kernel from its husk and for gathering a crop. What is inside a chest is described as being brought out and sorted, so hidden material is treated as a harvest.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Threshing was the last hard work of a season. Grain was beaten from the stalk, thrown into the wind, and what fell was the crop; the rest blew away. Everyone had stood in that dust. The verb the surah uses for what comes out of a chest is the verb for that separation, so the picture is not an interrogation but a winnowing.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah is one of a small number that open with a scene and never explain it. Five lines of cavalry at dawn arrive with no narrative attached and no identification of the riders, and the sixth line simply begins a statement about human nature. The classical commentators discuss the connection and record more than one account of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two hidden things are named as coming out on the same day, and they are paired deliberately: bodies from under the ground and contents from inside the chest. The second is the harder one, and the surah puts it last. Naming a person as the witness against himself also removes the possibility of a trial: what is produced as evidence is not an external record but the person's own knowledge of what he did.

crossReferences.why: States the same thing about self-witness explicitly, and adds that excuses will be offered anyway.
Names the same love of wealth and follows it to the same destination, a graveyard.
Applies the same phrase about the contents of chests to a specific moment of doubt in a community.

studies.applyIt: Count the things that went right for you yesterday before you count what went wrong. Do it in that order, out loud if you can. The word this surah uses for ingratitude describes someone who keeps an accurate ledger of losses and a vague one of gains, and the correction is not a feeling but an order of operations.
